titre: The cure that colonized a continent
accroche: 2,400 toads released in 1935 to protect sugarcane. They did not eat the pest, and there are now hundreds of millions of them
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1935, the sugarcane plantations of Queensland were suffering from a beetle whose larvae attack the roots. A solution proven elsewhere was imported from America: the cane toad, a large amphibian with a reputation for voracity.

About 2,400 individuals were released near Gordonvale.

Two details deserve to be noted from the outset. No impact study had been carried out. And no one had checked that the toad would actually eat that particular beetle.

## The problem of the encounter

It did not eat it, or so little.

The adult beetle lives at the top of the cane stalks, where a toad does not climb; its larvae are underground. The introduced animal and the targeted pest simply did not occupy the same space.

The toad, for its part, found everything else: soil insects, small vertebrates, scraps. It breeds by tens of thousands of eggs and tolerates drought and disturbed habitats.

Above all, it carries behind its eyes glands that secrete a violent poison. Australian predators, monitor lizards, quolls, snakes, freshwater crocodiles, share no evolutionary history with this toxin. They attack it, and they die.

The toad therefore advances without being eaten, and drives predators back in its path. It now occupies more than a million square kilometers, and the government classified it as an invasive species as early as 1950.

## What the invasion front produced

An unexpected result came from the speed of advance, which has kept increasing, by a factor of about five since arrival.

The explanation published in 2006 is evolutionary. In each generation, the individuals that move fastest arrive first at the front, and breed there with one another. The front thus selects, unintentionally, a more and more mobile offspring.

The toads at the front have longer legs than those of long-established populations. The invasion built its own accelerator.

A study covering eighty years, published in 2016, refines this picture: in the most recent front toads, it is the front legs that have strengthened, while the hind legs shortened, with a different mode of travel, by short, repeated hops rather than big single leaps. The accelerator, once launched, kept tuning itself.

## What the case cost to learn

The affair is cited as the textbook example of failed biological control, and it is. But the precise lesson deserves to be kept.

The mistake was not introducing a predator. It was reasoning about a function, “it eats insects,” rather than about a relationship: which insect, in what place, at what time, and what becomes of the animal once the job is done.

An organism does not perform a task. It lives, and it keeps living after the task.

repere.texte: The speed of advance of the invasion front has increased roughly fivefold since the toads arrived. Those at the front have longer legs than those of long-established populations.
repere.source: Phillips, Brown, Webb & Shine, “Invasion and the evolution of speed in toads,” Nature, 439, 2006

quiz.question: Why did the cane toad not regulate the targeted beetle?
choix: Because the adult insect lives at the top of the stalks and its larvae underground, out of reach
Because the toad turned out to be strictly herbivorous as an adult
Because the beetle had already disappeared by the time of the introduction
Because the toads released were too few to have an effect
quiz.explication: The introduced animal and the targeted pest did not occupy the same space: it is a matter of encounter, not of diet or numbers. The toad is indeed a voracious predator; it simply ate something else entirely, and prospered to the point of colonizing more than a million square kilometers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do Australian predators die when they attack the cane toad?
choix: Because they choke on an animal too big for them
Because they share no evolutionary history with its poison
Because the toad passes on a parasite imported from America
Because they neglect their usual prey and end up starving
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The toad carries behind its eyes glands that secrete a violent poison. Monitor lizards, quolls, snakes, and freshwater crocodiles never encountered this toxin in the course of their evolution: they attack it, and they die.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do we explain that the speed of the invasion front has kept increasing?
choix: The toads flee a growing heat and move south
Roads built since 1935 opened fast corridors for them
The most mobile individuals reach the front and breed there with one another
New introductions have regularly pushed the front westward
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The explanation published in 2006 is evolutionary: in each generation, those that move fastest arrive first at the front and breed there together. The invasion thus selects, unintentionally, a more and more mobile offspring.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the 2016 study show about toads at the most recent fronts?
choix: That their hind legs had kept lengthening without limit
That their poison had become harmless to local predators
That their front had stopped advancing after eighty years
That their front legs had strengthened and their hind legs shortened
quiz_supplementaire.explication: With eighty years of hindsight, the study refines the 2006 picture: in toads at the most recent fronts, the front legs have strengthened and the hind legs have shortened, with travel by short, repeated hops.
